subject: Allowing an individual variable to depend on state in CR model

messages.author: 7cb2eb89472f7169
messages.subject: Allowing an individual variable to depend on state in CR model
parts:
Hi all,

I’m trying to build a multistate capture-recapture (CR) model in which:

-        A quantitative individual variable (noted X, e.g. date of migration) between year t and t+1 is allowed to differ depending on the state in year t

-        One of the components of the transition probabilities from year t to year t+1 depends on X.

For most individuals, X is not available and is thus imputed.

The CR model works fine and produces reasonable results when the quantitative variables X depends on age and environmental covariates.

When X is allowed to depend on the state in year t (or at least that I try to do so), the model runs fine, but the results are somewhat surprising:  the posteriors of estimated differences in X depending on state are very narrow and centered on 0. Given the limited amount of data available, even if the differences in X between states are truly null, I expected that the posteriors would be much wider. I’m also unsure how to allow X to depend on state. Below is how I tried (omitting the effects of age and environmental covariates):

Let betai,t,k be the component of the transition probability (from t to t+1) that depends on Xi,t. k refers to the state in which individual i is in year t. Assuming there are two states k:

 

For the first state:

logit(beta[i, t, 1]) <- b[1] +

                                    b[2] * X[i, t, 1]

mu_X[i, t, 1] <- x[1]

X[i, t, 1] ~ dnorm(mu_X[i, t, 1], sd = sigma)

 

 

For the second state:

logit(beta[i, t, 2]) <- b[1] +

                                    b[2] * X[i, t, 2]

mu_X[i, t, 2] <- x[1] +  x[2]

 X[i, t, 2] ~ dnorm(mu_X[i, t, 2], sd = sigma) 

 

 

Note that X[i, t, 1] and X[i, t, 2] are the same: a matrix with as many lines as there are marked individuals, and as many columns as there are years, mostly filled with NAs, with only some individuals in some years for which X is known.

This way of specifying the model seems odd to me, but I couldn’t think of another way of allowing X to depend on state. I guess the fact that  X[i, t, 1] and X[i, t, 2]  are the same explains why the estimate of x[2] is so narrowly centered on 0.

What am I doing wrong here?

Attached is a simulated dataset (where x[2] = 1.5), the code of my CR model, and the fit of the model.

 

Thanks in advance,

Marwan

messages.author: d78486bfff620d81
messages.subject: Re: Allowing an individual variable to depend on state in CR model
parts:
Hi Marwan,

I'm having trouble understanding a few things in your description:

1) Does each individual in each year have their own state? If so, what variable in your model represents that state? You index `x` by state (1 or 2) but I don't see in your email where you denote the unknown state. I would think there should be something like `s[i,t]` that is a discrete variable taking possible values 1,2,...,max_number_states.
2) When you talk about transition probabilities, these are the probabilities of going from one state at time `t` to another state at time `t+1`, right? Is the 'state' that relates to the transition probabilities the same state you are talking about? If so, I would think you would have `beta[i, t, k1, k2]` indicating the probability of going from state k1 at time t to state k2 at time t+1 for individual i. 
3) I would think that an individual in year t would have a single unknown migration date, i.e., X[i,t] rather than X[i,t,k]. That date might have a different distribution depending on the state the individual is in. Just to give an example, perhaps `X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[s[i,t]], sd=sigma)` where `s[i,t]` is the state of individual i in year t.

My suggestions above are not meant to be concrete suggestions of how to change the model but just ideas to try to help think through what you are trying to do here.

-chris

Hi Chris,

Sorry for my delayed answer.

Thanks a lot for your answer! Sorry I tried to be both clear and concise, but I ended up not being clear enough.

1)     Does each individual in each year have their own state? If so, what variable in your model represents that state? You index `x` by state (1 or 2) but I don't see in your email where you denote the unknown state. I would think there should be something like `s[i,t]` that is a discrete variable taking possible values 1,2,...,max_number_states.
Correct. There are 12 states including the dead state in this model.

2)     When you talk about transition probabilities, these are the probabilities of going from one state at time `t` to another state at time `t+1`, right? Is the 'state' that relates to the transition probabilities the same state you are talking about? If so, I would think you would have `beta[i, t, k1, k2]` indicating the probability of going from state k1 at time t to state k2 at time t+1 for individual i.

Yes, by transition probabilities I did mean the probabilities of going from one state at time ‘t’ to another state at time ‘t+1’. And this 'state' is the state I was talking about. It would indeed make more sense to write beta as ‘beta[i, t, k1, k2]’, though beta is only one of the components of the transition probabilities (which is a product of several probabilities, e.g. surviving * migrating * breeding *…).

3)     I would think that an individual in year t would have a single unknown migration date, i.e., X[i,t] rather than X[i,t,k]. That date might have a different distribution depending on the state the individual is in. Just to give an example, perhaps `X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[s[i,t]], sd=sigma)` where `s[i,t]` is the state of individual i in year t.

Yes, an individual in year t has a single unknown migration date. The only reason I have X[i,t,k] instead of X[i, t] is because I was trying to figure out a way to allow X to depend on state. I previously tried to use a formulation like the one you propose (`X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[s[i,t]], sd=sigma)`), but it caused some issues which are related to another feature of my model that I did not describe: I actually have two quantitative variables X and W for each individual in each year: e.g. date of departure to wintering grounds + date of return to summering grounds. For the imputation of X and Y, I included a constraint: W > X + n days. I wanted to standardize values of X and W, so that the absolute value of coefficients would be small. But to ensure that once strandardized, values of W are still superior to values of X, I jointly standardized them (meaning we end up with values of X that are mostly < 0 and values of W that are mostly > 0, let’s call this ‘co-standardization’).

Back to the question at hand: the issue I encountered relates to the fact that for some states (most notably the dead state i.e. state 12), migration doesn’t occur. What prior should I specify for the intercept of mu_X[12] (considering I also included an effect of a continuous environmental variable)? I tried:

 

-        0: this leads to spurious results (even survival estimates were affected), which in foresight is not surprising given the mean of X (once co-standardized) is < 0. Imposing a value of 0 for mu_X[12] added a lot of information to the model, instead of not adding any, as I was intending.

-        NA: the model seems to run but the following warning messages are returned:

 

Warning: categorical sampler for 'z[4, 6]' encountered an invalid model density, and sampling results are likely invalid.

Warning: categorical sampler for 'z[9, 6]' encountered an invalid model density, and sampling results are likely invalid.

Warning: categorical sampler for 'z[10, 8]' encountered an invalid model density, and sampling results are likely invalid.

Etc.

 

-        The mean of X[1:n_individuals, 1:n_occasions] at each iteration: this produces the following error:

 

Error in permute.vertices(graph, oldGraphID_2_newGraphID) :

  At topology.c:2725 : Permute vertices: invalid permutation vector size, Invalid value

Calls: nimbleModel ... <Anonymous> -> genExpandedNodeAndParentNames3 -> permute.vertices

In addition: Warning message:

In topological.sort(graph, mode = "out") :

  At structural_properties.c:3346 :graph contains a cycle, partial result is returned

Execution halted

 

               Again, in foresight, this error is not really surprising since I’m asking to model to use X to compute X.

 

So, should I specify the same vague prior for the intercept of mu_X[12] as as I do for the intercepts of mu_X[1, 2, …., 11]? Will this ensure that dead individuals do not influence the estimation of the other parameters?

 

I hope everyhting makes sense.

Thanks in advance,

Marwan

parts:
Hi Marwan,

I am still a bit confused here in terms of notation. In your email you ask about `mu_X[12]`, where `mu_X` has a single index, but in your original code `mu_X` has three indices.

Assuming that you mean to have a single index, then for any state in which migration can occur, it makes sense to have something like `X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[z[i,t]], sd=sigma)`. This specification says that the migration date for individual i at time t will be on average the `mu_X` value associated with the state that that individual is currently in, which is `z[i,t]`.

However for state 12 (death) (and some other states, as you say), migration can't occur. This means that if the MCMC proposes `z[i,t]=12`, it should also be proposing to remove `X[i,t]` from the model in some sense. And when it proposes to go from `z[i,t]=12` to some other value for `z[i,t]` it needs to propose a value for `X[i,t]` as it is reentering the model. This changes the dimension of the parameter space. In some cases folks use reversible jump MCMC for this, though the technical details can get complicated.

We have a reversible jump sampler for variable selection in regression problems, but I doubt that one could use it directly in this case. 

I think the danger here in how you are trying to set things up is that `X[i,t]` is being treated as still in the model in proposing to move to `z[i,t]=12`.

Perhaps another way to think about this is to think about joint sampling for (X[i,t], Z[i,t]). If `Z[i,t]=12` is proposed, one also proposes to set `X[i,t]` to some "dummy" value, such as 99999, which has probability of 1 given `Z[i,t]=12`. Then if one proposes to set `Z[i,t]` to be something other than 12, one also proposes a value of `X[i,t]`, and acceptance depends on the joint density for the proposed `Z[i,t]` and `X[i,t]` values. This would involve setting up a user-defined specialized sampler and ensuring that it is a valid MCMC sampler.

It feels like others must have encountered such CR cases where one records other information about the captured individuals and wants to account for that in the modeling. I don't know this literature well, though. 

-chris

Hi Marwan,

I am still a bit confused here in terms of notation. In your email you ask about `mu_X[12]`, where `mu_X` has a single index, but in your original code `mu_X` has three indices.

Assuming that you mean to have a single index, then for any state in which migration can occur, it makes sense to have something like `X[i,t] ~ dnorm(mu_X[z[i,t]], sd=sigma)`. This specification says that the migration date for individual i at time t will be on average the `mu_X` value associated with the state that that individual is currently in, which is `z[i,t]`.

However for state 12 (death) (and some other states, as you say), migration can't occur. This means that if the MCMC proposes `z[i,t]=12`, it should also be proposing to remove `X[i,t]` from the model in some sense. And when it proposes to go from `z[i,t]=12` to some other value for `z[i,t]` it needs to propose a value for `X[i,t]` as it is reentering the model. This changes the dimension of the parameter space. In some cases folks use reversible jump MCMC for this, though the technical details can get complicated.

We have a reversible jump sampler for variable selection in regression problems, but I doubt that one could use it directly in this case. 

I think the danger here in how you are trying to set things up is that `X[i,t]` is being treated as still in the model in proposing to move to `z[i,t]=12`.

Perhaps another way to think about this is to think about joint sampling for (X[i,t], Z[i,t]). If `Z[i,t]=12` is proposed, one also proposes to set `X[i,t]` to some "dummy" value, such as 99999, which has probability of 1 given `Z[i,t]=12`. Then if one proposes to set `Z[i,t]` to be something other than 12, one also proposes a value of `X[i,t]`, and acceptance depends on the joint density for the proposed `Z[i,t]` and `X[i,t]` values. This would involve setting up a user-defined specialized sampler and ensuring that it is a valid MCMC sampler.

It feels like others must have encountered such CR cases where one records other information about the captured individuals and wants to account for that in the modeling. I don't know this literature well, though. 

-chris
